title: Designing a video streaming service like Netflix

facts.text: Users stream and share videos, search by title or tag and comment, while the content team uploads new videos; the system needs high availability with minimal latency, high reliability so no uploads are lost, and scalability.
Extended requirements are geo-blocking of certain content, resuming playback from where the user left off, and recording video metrics and analytics.

The read-heavy estimate assumes 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 videos watched a day: 1 billion videos per day, 5 million uploads per day at a 200:1 read/write ratio, and 12K requests per second.
At 100 MB per video, about 500 TB of storage is needed every day and about 1,825 PB over 10 years, with a minimum ingress bandwidth of around 5.8 GB per second.
Tables hold users, videos (title, streamURL, tags, userID), tags, views and comments; each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra.

Upload takes a title, description, byte stream and optional tags; stream takes a video ID, codec, resolution and optional offset in seconds; search takes a query and optional next-page token; add comment takes a video ID and text.
Microservices each own their data model: user, stream, search, media (uploads and processing) and analytics services, communicating over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.
Two-hour raw 8K footage can reach 4 TB, so uploads are queued in a message queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ: processing is a long-running task and the queue decouples it from uploading.

A file chunker splits video by scene, not equal timestamps, so a requested chunk is less likely to be interrupted; a machine-learning content filter checks copyright, piracy and NSFW, sending problems to a dead-letter queue.

A transcoder decodes to an intermediate format and re-encodes with different codecs (FFmpeg or AWS Elemental MediaConvert); quality conversion yields 4K, 1440p, 1080p and 720p, stored in HDFS, GlusterFS or an object store such as Amazon S3.

A CDN stops users re-fetching content; Netflix's Open Connect partners with thousands of ISPs, delivers around 95% of traffic over direct ISP connections from appliances in over 1000 locations, and fails over to Netflix servers.
Adaptive bitrate protocols such as HLS adapt playback to network conditions; to resume playback, the offset stored in the views table retrieves the scene chunk at that timestamp.
Search runs on Elasticsearch; trending content comes from caching the most frequently searched queries of the last N seconds and refreshing them every M seconds with a batch job.

Geo-blocking, driven by legal distribution rights, finds the user's location by IP or profile region and redirects blocked users to an error page; a machine-learning model predicts what to watch next from viewing history.
Cache static media with Redis or Memcached using LRU eviction, falling back to the database on a miss; shard horizontally, using consistent hashing against uneven distribution.

To remove single points of failure, run multiple instances of each service, place load balancers between clients, servers, databases and cache servers, use read replicas and replicate the distributed cache.

notes: Left out for the 16-fact cap: sharing links with a URL shortener (fc7022253b61), metrics with Spark (c766841deb00), content-policy details. Open Connect and geo-blocking have their own entries. Chunk 2 holds only Wikipedia concept pages, so the worked solution does not span chunks.

title: Live streaming

definition.text: Delivering video over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds.

facts.text: Live streaming differs from regular streaming because the video is sent over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds.
The camera and microphone capture raw video, which goes to the server side to be compressed and encoded to a standard such as H.264, making the data much smaller.
Encoded data is divided into segments, usually seconds long, so it takes much less time to download or stream.
The streaming server must support different devices and network conditions, which means adaptive bitrate streaming and producing multiple files at different bitrates when encoding and segmenting.
Live data is pushed to CDN edge servers so millions of viewers can watch from a nearby edge server, which significantly lowers transmission latency.
Viewers' devices decode and decompress the data and play it in a player; for replay, the encoded data is also sent to a storage server that viewers can request from later.

RTMP, developed by Macromedia for Flash players and now used to stream video over the internet, HLS (needing H.264 or H.265) and DASH are standard protocols; HLS and DASH both support adaptive bitrate streaming.
Video conferencing applications such as Skype use real-time communication (RTC) protocols for lower latency.

title: Video transcoding

definition.text: Converting video by decoding it to an intermediate uncompressed format and re-encoding it into a target format and quality for different devices.

facts.text: Transcoding is a two-step process: the original data is decoded to an intermediate uncompressed format (YUV for video), which is then encoded into the target format.

It is used when a target device does not support the format or has limited storage; codecs adjust the bitrate, downsample images or re-encode the media into a smaller file in a format better optimized for the target.

Raw video is transcoded into different compression rates and resolutions for different devices, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k), so the requested quality can be fetched.
Transrating lowers the bitrate without changing the video format, while transsizing changes the picture size when the output resolution differs from the source.
The diversity of mobile devices and their capabilities makes transcoding a must in mobile content adaptation.

Transcoding to a lossy format reduces quality, and compression artifacts are cumulative, so each generation loses more (digital generation loss); it can be lossless if the output is losslessly compressed or uncompressed.
To minimize loss, treat the original recording as the master copy and transcode each desired version only from that master, since any transcoding involves some cumulative image loss.
Standalone tools such as FFmpeg or cloud services such as AWS Elemental MediaConvert can implement the transcoding step of a video pipeline.

title: Geo-blocking

definition.text: Technology that restricts access to Internet content based on the user's geographical location.

facts.text: The user's location is found mainly from the IP address, mapped to a country or region with GeoIP databases; GPS queries, accounts and network delay measurements are also used. The result approves or denies access.

Netflix and YouTube restrict content by region: on Netflix mainly because of legal distribution laws tied to deals with producers and distributors, on YouTube because the publisher chooses when publishing.

Blocking can be network-level, filtering IP packets, or application-level, denying access after detecting the location; CDNs often integrate geo-blocking controls, and AWS offers CloudFront geographic restrictions or Route 53 geolocation routing.
IP-to-location mapping is inaccurate and its databases must be kept current, and VPN or proxy services let users evade IP-based geo-blocks by appearing in another country.

title: YouTube's video transcoding unit

definition.text: YouTube built a dedicated chip, the VCU, to transcode its uploads because software encoding had become slow and costly.

facts.text: YouTube handles 500+ hours of uploaded video every minute on average.
Its job is to transcode raw video into different compression rates for different viewing devices, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k).
Software-based encoding became slow and costly, so a processor specialized for video encoding and decoding was needed.

YouTube developed the VCU (Video transCoding Unit) for warehouse-scale video processing, as GPUs and TPUs serve graphics and machine learning: clusters of VCU servers, with accelerator trays of cards holding encoders and decoders.
The VCU cluster generates the different resolutions and stores them in cloud storage; the design gave 20-33x improvements in computing efficiency over the previous optimized system.

title: Netflix Open Connect

definition.text: Netflix's purpose-built content delivery network, which places appliances at partner internet service providers.

facts.text: Open Connect is a purpose-built CDN responsible for serving Netflix's video traffic, going a step further than a traditional CDN.
Netflix partners with thousands of internet service providers (ISPs) to localize its traffic and deliver content more efficiently.
Around 95% of traffic globally is delivered via direct connections between Open Connect and the ISPs customers use to reach the internet.
Open Connect Appliances (OCAs) sit in over 1000 separate locations around the world.
If an appliance has issues it can fail over, and traffic is re-routed to Netflix servers.

title: Netflix's technology stack

definition.text: The languages, frameworks, databases and data tools behind Netflix's apps and services.

facts.text: Netflix builds native mobile apps in Swift and Kotlin and its web application in React, and uses GraphQL for frontend-server communication.
Backend services rely on ZUUL, Eureka, the Spring Boot framework and other technologies.
Databases include EVCache, Cassandra and CockroachDB; video is stored on S3 and served through Open Connect.
Kafka and Flink handle messaging and streaming; Flink and Spark process data, visualized with Tableau, and Redshift holds structured data warehouse information.
CI/CD relies on tools such as Jenkins, Gradle, Spinnaker and Chaos Monkey.

title: Adaptive bitrate streaming

definition.text: A technique that encodes video at several bit rates and lets the player switch between them as bandwidth, CPU and device conditions change.

facts.text: It works by detecting the user's bandwidth, CPU capability and device type in real time and adjusting the quality of the stream, giving little buffering, faster start times and a good experience on high-end and low-end connections.
An encoder encodes one source at multiple bit rates and each stream is segmented into small multi-second parts; the client first downloads a manifest describing the segments and their bit rates.
The client starts with the lowest bit rate stream, requests a higher bit rate when throughput exceeds the downloaded segment's bit rate, and a lower one when throughput deteriorates.
The client's ABR algorithm decides which segments to download: throughput-based algorithms use recent download throughput, buffer-based ones use only the buffer level, and hybrid ones combine both.
Today's adaptive technologies are based almost exclusively on HTTP, replacing stateful single-bitrate protocols such as RTP with RTSP.
Because it is built on HTTP, packets traverse firewalls and NAT, the client drives adaptation so the server keeps no per-client session state, and existing HTTP caches and servers can be used.

Delivered over HTTP through content delivery networks it scales to millions of concurrent viewers, edge servers need only simple HTTP server software, and the CDN cost resembles that of HTTP web caching.
It needs additional encoding, adds storage and encoding costs, and is more complex to operate than traditional streaming; no single standard exists for digital rights management across the methods.

title: HTTP Live Streaming

definition.text: A protocol for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data over HTTP, in which the client downloads a playlist and the media segments it lists, adapting bit rate to network conditions.

facts.text: HLS is an HTTP-based protocol from Apple for live and on-demand video; version 7 is specified in RFC 8216, and a receiver can adapt the bit rate to current network conditions to keep playback uninterrupted.

A presentation is a URI to a UTF-8 text Playlist. A Media Playlist lists the Media Segments to play in sequence; a Master Playlist lists Variant Streams, each the same content at a particular bit rate, format and resolution.

A segmenter, also called a packager, cuts the media into segments no longer than a constant target duration, typically 10 seconds, each with its own URI, in MPEG-2 Transport Stream, fragmented MP4, packed audio or WebVTT subtitle format.
Each segment has a unique Media Sequence Number, one higher than the segment before it, and the server announces each segment's duration in the playlist, so clients can order and locate segments.

For seamless switching between Variant Streams, each must present the same content with matching timestamps and the same target duration; clients switch variants to adapt to the network and pick Renditions, such as audio languages, by user preference.

A live playlist is only appended to or trimmed from the front, with EXT-X-MEDIA-SEQUENCE incremented per removed segment and at least three target durations left; the server adds EXT-X-ENDLIST when the final segment is published.

The client downloads the playlist, then each segment in order, and reloads the playlist to find new segments: it waits at least one target duration after a changed reload and half that after an unchanged one.

Because it is plain HTTP, it works with large-scale HTTP caching infrastructure for big audiences; segments can be encrypted, with an EXT-X-KEY tag pointing to a key file whose delivery SHOULD be secured with TLS.

notes: Replaces the first-round entry: RFC 8216 is the standard-tier source for how HLS works, so it becomes the article. The ByteByteGo claim that HLS requires H.264 or H.265 encoding (4ac1d0eefb1d) is left out: the RFC lists supported segment formats and a CODECS attribute but sets no codec requirement.

title: MPEG-DASH

definition.text: Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, an international-standard adaptive bitrate technique that streams media from conventional HTTP web servers.

facts.text: Content is split into small segments served over HTTP, each a short slice of playback time, and offered at several bit rates as alternative segments covering aligned intervals.

During playback the client's adaptation algorithm picks the highest-bit-rate segment that can be downloaded in time to avoid stalls or re-buffering, so it adapts seamlessly to changing network conditions.
The standard does not specify the adaptation logic; the reference client dash.js offers buffer-based (BOLA) and hybrid (DYNAMIC) bit rate adaptation algorithms.

A media presentation description (MPD) describes each segment's timing, URL and media characteristics such as resolution and bit rate; segments use the ISO base media file format (such as MP4) or MPEG-2 Transport Stream.

DASH reuses existing HTTP web server infrastructure and needs no special server support except for live streaming; it is not a transport protocol, running over TCP with HTTP and HTTP/2, or over QUIC with HTTP/3.

DASH was developed under MPEG and published as ISO/IEC 23009-1:2012 in April 2012; standardizing assures the market it works universally, unlike vendor-specific solutions, and it is codec-agnostic (H.265, H.264, VP9).
Netflix and YouTube support MPEG-DASH; it is not directly supported in HTML5, so JavaScript players use the Media Source Extensions, and DRM works through the Encrypted Media Extensions.

The Common Media Application Format (CMAF) container is intended to simplify delivering both HLS and MPEG-DASH; of the HTTP-based adaptive implementations, only these two are still actively developed and used in 2026.

title: Streaming media

definition.text: Delivering multimedia over a network as a stream of packets that is played in real time or near real time, instead of downloading the whole file first.

facts.text: Media is transferred as a stream of packets from a server to a client and rendered in real time or near real time, unlike downloading, where the user obtains the entire file before consuming it.
Live streaming is the real-time delivery of content during production, much as live television broadcasts content.

Streams are compressed with video coding formats such as H.264, HEVC, VP8, VP9 and AV1, assembled into a container such as MP4 or WebM, and delivered from a streaming server using a transport protocol such as RTMP or RTP.
In the 2010s HLS, Smooth Streaming, HDS and the non-proprietary MPEG-DASH emerged to provide adaptive bitrate streaming over HTTP as an alternative to proprietary transport protocols.
A broadband speed of 2 Mbit/s or more is recommended for standard-definition video, 5 Mbit/s for high-definition and 25 Mbit/s for ultra-high-definition content.
Storage size in megabytes is length in seconds × bit rate in bit/s / (8 × 1024 × 1024); one hour of video encoded at 300 kbit/s needs around 128 MB.

UDP sends the stream as small packets, simple and efficient but with no delivery guarantee, so the application must recover from loss; TCP guarantees delivery but stalls the stream on loss, which client buffering softens.
Buffering delay is acceptable for video on demand, but interactive applications such as video conferencing lose fidelity if buffering delay exceeds 200 ms.

title: Streaming delivery methods

definition.text: The ways a stream reaches many viewers: separate unicast copies, a single multicast stream, peer-to-peer transfer, or CDN servers.

facts.text: Unicast sends a separate copy of the stream to each recipient; it is the norm on the Internet but does not scale when many users want the same program at once.
For a 300 kbit/s stream viewed by 1,000 people over unicast, the server needs 300 Mbit/s; with multicast it sends one common stream using only 300 kbit/s.
Multicast sends a single stream from the source to a group of recipients, cutting server and network load, but may not be feasible on every network and loses video on demand functionality.

Peer-to-peer protocols send prerecorded streams between computers so the server and its connections do not become a bottleneck, but raise technical, performance, security, quality and business issues; CDNs instead use intermediate servers to distribute the load.

title: Recommender system

definition.text: A type of information filtering system that suggests the items most relevant to a particular user, such as what to watch next.

facts.text: Recommender systems generate playlists for streaming services, product suggestions for e-commerce and items on social media; they matter where users face many options, and help users discover items they might not have found by search.

Collaborative filtering builds a model from a user's past behavior and similar decisions by other users; content-based filtering uses pre-tagged characteristics of items to recommend others with similar properties.

Collaborative filtering needs a lot of data about a user, the cold start problem; content-based filtering needs very little to start but is limited in scope, recommending only items similar to the seed.
Collaborative filtering often suffers from cold start, scalability and sparsity; a commonly implemented solution to cold start is the multi-armed bandit algorithm.

Most systems are hybrids that combine collaborative, content-based and other approaches, for example by weighted scores, switching, mixed presentation, cascading or meta-level models; hybrids can be more accurate than pure approaches and ease cold start and sparsity.

Streaming services recommend from each user's view history together with all viewers' aggregated histories, extrapolating early viewers' choices to the whole user base; Netflix uses a hybrid of similar users' habits and titles resembling those a user rated highly.

Netflix's engine tracks profile information, browsing and scrolling behavior, time and date of viewing, the device used, and the number of searches and search terms, feeding a machine learning model on viewing history.

In the two-tower model for candidate retrieval, a user tower and an item tower produce embeddings in a shared vector space; relevance is a dot product or cosine similarity, and item embeddings can be pre-computed.

title: Collaborative filtering

definition.text: A recommendation technique that predicts a user's interests from the preferences of many other users, assuming people who agreed before will agree again.

facts.text: It predicts a user's interests from taste information collected from many users, assuming that two people who share opinions on one issue are likelier to agree on others than a random pairing.
The prediction is specific to the user but uses information from many users, unlike the simpler approach of giving every item one average score, for example from its number of votes.

User-based filtering finds users with rating patterns like the active user's and predicts from their ratings; item-based filtering ('users who bought x also bought y') builds an item-item matrix and matches the user's data against it.
Instead of explicit ratings it can use implicit observations of behavior, such as what a user listened to or bought, together with what all users did, to predict future behavior.

Memory-based methods compute user or item similarity from ratings (Pearson correlation, cosine similarity) and predict a weighted average of neighbors' ratings; model-based methods learn a model, such as singular value decomposition latent factors, that compresses the sparse user-item matrix.

Memory-based filtering is explainable, easy to build and independent of item content, but performance drops when data is sparse and adding items means re-inserting elements in the structure; most commercial systems are hybrids of both kinds.

Key challenges are cold start (new users or items lack data), sparsity of the huge user-item matrix, and scalability, since traditional algorithms struggle with tens of millions of customers and millions of items.

Open rating systems invite shilling attacks, with positive ratings for one's own items and negative ones for competitors', so precautions are needed; and because it recommends from past ratings it favors popular products, a rich-get-richer effect.

title: Video codec

definition.text: Software or hardware that compresses and decompresses digital video, usually following a standard video coding format.

facts.text: A codec is an encoder and a decoder in one; raw video needs too much storage and bandwidth, so codecs make it feasible to record, transmit and stream it.

Video compression is typically lossy, so decompressed video has lower quality than the original; the bit rate trades off against quality, algorithm complexity, sensitivity to errors, random access and latency.

Encoding usually converts the image to YCbCr and subsamples the less perceptually important chroma, applies a transform (the 8x8 DCT is most popular), quantizes the output, then entropy-encodes the values.
Decoding inverts each stage of encoding as far as possible, but quantization is inherently non-invertible, so decoding only approximates it.
Standards specify only the decoding process; encoders are free to differ, so video quality can vary dramatically between encoders that use the same codec standard.
The trade-off between compression power, speed and fidelity, including artifacts, is usually the most important measure of a codec's technical merit.

Since H.261, DCT compression has been adopted by all major video coding standards; H.264/AVC was the most widely used format as of 2016, with HEVC as its successor and the open, free VP8, VP9 and AV1 as alternatives.

title: Real-Time Messaging Protocol

definition.text: A protocol for streaming audio, video and data over the Internet, originally built by Macromedia for Flash Player and running over TCP.

facts.text: RTMP runs on TCP, port 1935 by default, with persistent connections for low latency; after a handshake of three packets from each side, streams are split into fragments of dynamically negotiated size (default 64 bytes for audio, 128 for video).

Packets from several independent virtual channels, such as RPC, video, audio and control messages, are interleaved and multiplexed over a single connection so each channel meets its bandwidth and latency needs.
Variants include RTMPS (over TLS), RTMPE (Adobe's encryption), RTMPT (tunneled in HTTP on ports 80 and 443 to pass firewalls) and RTMFP (over UDP instead of TCP).

The codec selection of FLV and RTMP is limited, so the industry extended it; Enhanced RTMP adds multitrack, expanded codec support, FourCC signaling and a reconnect request while staying compatible with existing RTMP infrastructure.

title: Video on demand

definition.text: A media distribution system that lets users access television shows, films and videos digitally on request.

facts.text: A selected video can begin playing immediately (streaming) or be downloaded for deferred viewing; streaming has become the more popular way to provide it.
Some systems store programs on hard disks and use a memory buffer so the user can fast-forward and rewind; video servers on local networks give rapid responses.
Business models include subscription (SVOD, a regular fee for unlimited programs), transactional (TVOD, a fee per title) and advertising-based (AVOD, free to viewers).

Near video on demand broadcasts copies of a programme at staggered intervals, typically every 10-20 minutes, which is bandwidth-intensive; push VOD pre-loads popular content onto the viewer's set-top box to optimize the streaming infrastructure.

title: H.264

definition.text: Advanced Video Coding (AVC, H.264, MPEG-4 Part 10), a block-oriented, motion-compensated video compression standard.

facts.text: H.264 is by far the most commonly used format for recording, compression and distribution of video, used by 79% of video industry developers as of December 2024, including streaming services such as Netflix, YouTube and Vimeo.
Bit rate savings of 50% or more over MPEG-2 Part 2 are reported: the same digital satellite TV quality at 1.5 Mbit/s for H.264 against around 3.5 Mbit/s for MPEG-2.

Profiles define sets of capabilities for classes of applications, High Profile being by far the most used; a level sets the maximum resolution, frame rate and bit rate, and a conforming decoder also decodes all lower levels.

H.264 is patent-restricted and commercial use requires royalties; software encoders on general-purpose CPUs are less power-efficient than hardware, but compression efficiency depends on the algorithm, so the difference is power, flexibility and cost.

chapter: Design a video streaming service like Netflix

title: HEVC

definition.text: High Efficiency Video Coding (H.265, MPEG-H Part 2), a patent-encumbered video compression standard published in 2013 as the successor to H.264/AVC.

facts.text: HEVC achieves 25% to 50% better compression than AVC at the same quality; 4K at 30 frames per second needs about 50 Mbps and 22.5 GB per hour, against 100 Mbps and 45 GB for older H.264 profiles.

It extends AVC's idea of finding redundant areas within and between frames, using coding tree units up to 64x64 samples instead of 16x16 macroblocks; this needs much more signal processing to compress but has less impact on decompression.
HEVC supports resolutions up to 8192x4320, including 8K UHD, and improved parallel processing through tiles and wavefront parallel processing.

Combined licensing fees from the patent bodies are higher than for AVC, which is a main reason HEVC adoption on the web has been low and why large companies joined the Alliance for Open Media, which finalized the royalty-free AV1.

chapter: Design a video streaming service like Netflix

title: AV1

definition.text: AOMedia Video 1, an open, royalty-free video coding format from the Alliance for Open Media, designed for video transmission over the Internet as the successor to VP9.

facts.text: AV1 is royalty-free, unlike H.264 and H.265, so it does not hinder open-source adoption; its alliance was motivated by the high cost and uncertainty of HEVC patent licensing.
It is a block-based frequency transform format built on VP9 that gives encoders more coding options; frames are divided into superblocks of 128×128 or 64×64 pixels, and it targets lossy encoding.
Its payoff is bandwidth: Netflix's 2017 tests found AV1 about 25% more efficient than VP9, and Netflix's 2020 Android streams gave 20% improved compression efficiency over its VP9 streams.
The cost is compute: in a 2020 study AV1 encodes at 2160p took on average 590× longer than AVC (VP9 5.2×, HEVC 4.2×), and 2017 decoding ran at about half the speed of VP9.

notes: Early comparisons disagreed (a late-2016 test found AV1 65.7% less efficient than HEVC, 807e46813eb9; later tests found it at least as good, f5f09f0f5d9f); they used different encoder versions and settings, so no conflict is recorded and only the later Netflix and Waterloo figures are stated.
